title: Graeme Halford: Relational Complexity

html:
Graeme Halford’s theories introduced some interesting objections to Case’s theory. His core objection to Case is that "working memory capacity" isn’t a single executive resource you can read off from task difficulty, because two people can face the same task yet represent it differently (different goals, chunking, latent variables). So he shifts the explanation of cognitive growth from "how much executive capacity do you have?" to "what relational structure can you hold and map into a coherent mental model?" Essentially, he argued that development is less about raw buffer size and more about the maximum relational arity (how many entities/relations) your internal simulator can bind at once without collapsing into heuristics or memorized templates.

His central mechanism is structure mapping: you understand new problems by translating them into a familiar relational schema (an internal model) via analogy, suggesting that intelligence scales with the ability to align incoming data with high-dimensional internal graphs. What limits you, then, is relational complexity: the number of distinct entities/dimensions that must be simultaneously represented for the relations to be understood (not just recognized). A simple comparison like "A is larger than B" is a binary relation (two entities + one relation). A transitive inference like "A > B and B > C, so A > C" forces you to coordinate three entities and two relations at once; if you can’t keep that whole structure active, you won’t reliably derive the implied relation. A relational-complexity experiment varies the relations in matrix problems (Figure) 1. The experiment controls task order and complexity (Figure).

Halford’s four levels are basically a ladder of "how many slots in the relational graph can you bind simultaneously," often linked to  1, 3, 5, and  10 years (and aligning roughly with Piaget/Case stage labels):

Unary / element mappings ( 1y; sensorimotor) are about single-attribute matches

In perception/objects, "this is an apple" from shape or color; in social, "smiling face = happy," "loud voice = scary." Actions at this stage are basic stimulus-response mappings.

Case Equivalent: Sensorimotor Stage (The "unit" is a raw input/output).

The agent binds a specific attribute to an entity. It validates existence but not relation.

Binary / relational mappings ( 3y; preoperational) add dyadic relations

In space/physics, "the block is on the box," "this door is bigger than that opening"; in social, "Mom likes me," "he is meaner than her," or simple ownership ("that’s mine").

Case Equivalent: Interrelational Stage (The "unit" is a relationship between sensorimotor units).

This is the minimum complexity required for simple feedback loops where StatecurrentState_{current} is compared to StategoalState_{goal}.

System mappings ( 5y; concrete operational) handle ternary structure or the integration of two relations

In math, solving "3 + ? = 8" requires coordinating (3, ?, 8) under one operation; in causal/spatial reasoning, transitivity and constraints like "if A blocks B and B blocks C, moving B frees C," or "A fits in B, B fits in C ⇒ A fits in C" (containment chains).

This corresponds to Case’s Dimensional stage, where the "unit" is a quantitative variable

This is the first stage where variables are abstract

Multiple-system mappings ( 10y; formal operational / vectorial) support quaternary structure-relations between relations: in math/physics, proportionality and ratios ("gear A:B = 2:1 and B:C = 3:1 ⇒ A:C = 6:1"), or balancing two unknowns under constraints; in social/strategy, reasoning about "what I believe you believe she intends" (nested mental-state models) or coordinating multiple interacting rules ("if we choose plan X, it helps goal G but violates constraint K unless we add step S"). This level of complexity is required for abstract analogy and proportionality.

Halford is basically proposing a capacity metric for model-based reasoning that’s not "tokens in a buffer," but "maximum relational complexity of the latent graph you can stably instantiate and manipulate." Scaling up cognition then looks like (1) learning better schemas to map into (better priors / reusable world-model fragments), and (2) increasing the system’s ability to bind higher-arity relations (more simultaneous variables/constraints) without losing coherence-exactly the difference between a model that recognizes patterns and a model that can do robust planning, counterfactuals, and multi-constraint control across domains. The relational-complexity experiment measures performance (Figure). The experiment also maps brain responses (Figure).

It may seem that Halford’s theory is redundant with respect to Case’s theory; however, Halford adds a sharper task-analytic metric for what "capacity" must actually support: the maximum relational arity (unary -> binary -> ternary -> quaternary) that can be simultaneously bound for a concept to be intelligible. Where Case explains developmental growth via practice-driven compilation of ECS components (freeing resources to build higher-order units like dimensions and vectors), Halford tells you how to count the minimal structure the world model must co-instantiate (how many entities, relations, and relations-between-relations must be live at once) independent of domain content or strategy. Essentially, Case is the growth mechanism (compression/automation increases effective bandwidth), while Halford is the constraint and measurement lens: it predicts exactly which problems will collapse into heuristics or memorization when relational complexity exceeds the agent’s current binding capacity, and it lets you compare "difficulty" across domains by the structure of the underlying graph, not by superficial features of the task. Halford argues that "number of items" (storage) is irrelevant if they aren’t interacting. He cares about the dimensionality of the active graph, which is about parallelism. It doesn’t matter if you can store 10 variables; if you can only compute the interaction of 3 at a time, you literally cannot represent a quaternary relation (like a proportion of proportions) without collapsing the waveform. Another way of putting it: Halford provides the architecture (the "what"; the data structures): he tells you that "intelligence" is the ability to process higher-rank tensors (relations of relations). Case provides the learning rule (the "how"; the optimization process): he tells you that the only way to afford those expensive higher-rank tensors is by compressing the lower-rank ones into efficient sub-routines. Practice compresses "Search" (high compute) into "Lookup" (low compute); from high- to low-dimensional. Structure mapping is a key mechanism for such compression.
